output.headline: Nearly half a million people choose wildlife for new UK banknotes
output.standfirst: Barn owls, bumblebees, puffins and hedgehogs were voted onto Britain’s next banknotes, after dropping historical figures such as Churchill drew political criticism, while the RSPCA said the shortlist needed less obviously cute creatures.
output.bodyHtml:
Barn owls, bumblebees, puffins and hedgehogs have been chosen by the public to feature on the next generation of Bank of England banknotes, after a consultation in which nearly half a million people took part – though the decision to retire historical figures such as Winston Churchill and Jane Austen prompted a backlash from opposition politicians.

Victoria Cleland, the Bank's chief cashier, said: "I am delighted that nearly half-a-million people responded to our wildlife imagery consultation, showing that cash still matters." She said the public had chosen "four distinct and inspiring animals" that not only showcased the great variety of wildlife in the UK but would "also enhance the security of our banknotes".

The quartet of creatures were selected after a large-scale consultation settled on wild animals as the theme, with members of the public then asked to pick their favourites out of 18 options divided into three categories.

The buff-tailed bumblebee got the most votes in the insects, fish and amphibian group; the barn owl won the bird division; and the European hedgehog was named top mammal. The Atlantic puffin was added to celebrate Britain's coastline, the Bank said.

It is as yet undecided which species will adorn which banknote. An image of King Charles will continue to be represented on the other side of the £5, £10, £20 and £50 notes, which are expected to take several years to design.

Among the species losing out were the basking shark, the common frog and the red fox – the latter celebrated in David Attenborough's recent Wild London documentary, but seen as a pest by some.

Atlantic puffins, with their distinctive multicoloured beaks, spend much of their lives at sea, coming ashore in summer to nest in burrows on islands off the coast including the Farne Islands and Lundy.

With their numbers declining, the bird is classified as "vulnerable" on the International Union for Conservation of Nature's red list of threatened species.

The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, accused the Bank of "erasing our history" after the decision to replace the historical figures on the banknotes – including Winston Churchill and Jane Austen – was first announced in March. Badenoch called it "a silly thing to do", adding: "I absolutely do not support it." Her Reform UK counterpart, Nigel Farage, described the move as "absolutely crackers".

The Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, joined in, issuing a social media video in which he brandished a fiver and claimed that Churchill deserved "better than being replaced by a badger".

The badger was not among the 18-strong shortlist of animals eventually published by the Bank in June.

That selection prompted the RSPCA to complain about the choice of animals on offer, calling for less obviously cute creatures to be included. "Gulls, badgers, rats and pigeons all divide opinion, but this would have been a great opportunity to discuss these fantastic animals," it said.
output.progress: The Bank of England says the chosen designs will also strengthen banknote security as it finalises which creature appears on which note.
